simple: several pretend computers made inside one real computer, so you can practise cluster work without a cluster.
analogy: three friends who play at living in different towns by sitting in three rooms of one house and passing letters under the doors.
precise: a set of virtual machines, containers or processes on one host that each act as a node, with separate address spaces and network connections between them; it reproduces the software interfaces of a cluster but not its independence: the nodes share the host's CPUs, clock, kernel (for processes) and power. In BR-10 each node is a process reached over a loopback TCP connection.
source: R2 of BR-10 (lab run, g++ 13.3.0); D3 of BR-10 (van Steen and Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the one helper who is much slower than the others, so everyone waits for them at the end.
analogy: a friend who sorts at a table shared with noisy cousins, so the whole group waits for her box.
precise: a node or task that finishes much later than its peers, so that the completion time of a parallel job, the maximum over its parts, is set by it; causes include a shared or overloaded node, a slow disk or link, or an uneven share of the work.
source: R5 and R14 of BR-10 (lab runs); D2 of BR-10 (Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", ch. 8) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: either everyone gets their pile at the start, or everyone comes back for the next piece when they finish.
analogy: posting three equal boxes of stamps at once, or posting one small box at a time to whoever has written back.
precise: in fixed (static) assignment, task t goes to worker t mod n before the run starts, as in a block or cyclic decomposition by rank; in dynamic assignment (self-scheduling), an idle worker receives the next pending task, so faster workers do more tasks. Dynamic assignment absorbs stragglers at the cost of one message per task.
source: R3 and R5 of BR-10 (lab runs); D3 of BR-10 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: waiting for an answer with no point at which you give up.
analogy: waiting a whole month for a friend's letter before phoning to ask.
precise: a blocking call (a receive, a poll, a collective operation) made without a deadline; if the peer stalls while its connection stays open, nothing wakes the caller and the program hangs without an error.
source: R6 and R10 of BR-10 (lab runs, exit code 124 from timeout); D2 of BR-10 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: asking another computer for its time and using how long the question took to judge how wrong its clock is.
analogy: phoning a friend, noting the time when you ask and when they answer, and assuming their answer was spoken half-way between.
precise: an estimate of the offset between a remote clock and the local clock: send a request at local time t0, receive the remote reading T at local time t1, and take T - (t0 + t1)/2; the error is at most (t1 - t0)/2, so the probe with the shortest round trip is kept. The reasoning behind Cristian's method (F5-10).
source: D3 of BR-10 (van Steen and Tanenbaum, clock synchronization) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R8 of BR-10 (lab run with injected offsets)

simple: making sure a computer you have given up on really stops, so it cannot do harm later.
analogy: asking a friend's town to close his post office until he has been checked.
precise: forcibly isolating a suspected node (powering it off through its management controller, cutting its storage or network access) before its work is given to others, so that a node that was only slow cannot later write stale results; fencing tokens are the software counterpart at the receiving side.
source: D2 of BR-10 (Kleppmann, ch. 8, fencing) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R7 of BR-10 (SIGKILL as a stand-in for a BMC power-off)
